paragraphs.text: Many and great are the gifts of God, the lover of mankind, but the first and greatest of all his gifts is the teaching of the Scriptures. The sun and moon, the whole chorus of the stars, the rivers, springs and lakes came into being to care for our bodies. The holy Scriptures were given to set our souls right. As far as the soul is above the body, so far is the gift of the divine Scriptures above all other gifts. That is why the Saviour says: "Search the Scriptures, for in them you think you have eternal life." So let us search the treasures of the Scriptures, take hold of the promise, and try, as far as we are able, to explain the creation of man. And once again, let no one find fault with questions that are examined carefully. Finding fault with God's ordinances and attacking what is said with precision is typical of people who are set on idle chatter. I have heard some people complain: what need was there to talk about fire and water, about how fire crackles when water is thrown on it? "We," one of them says, "do not want to learn natural science; we want theology." But you should know that such words come from idle and lazy people. Next to theology, natural science lays a foundation for piety. If they throw out natural science, let them bring charges against the prophets and blame the apostles. The apostle speaks of nature: "Not all flesh is the same flesh. There is one flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fish, another of birds; and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies." Why does Paul speak of nature and argue from musical instruments, saying: "There are, it may be, so many kinds of sounds in the world, and none is without meaning"? "For if the trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will get ready for battle? Whether flute or harp, if it gives no distinction between the notes, how will anyone know what is being played on the flute or the harp?" What did Paul's tongue have to do with the flute and the harp? Yet he speaks of nature from visible things in order to present the things grasped by the mind. What need was there for so much natural science in the book of Job? "The strength of the lion, the voice of the lioness, the pride of serpents is quenched. The ant-lion perished for lack of food." "The young of vultures fly to the heights." Why did another prophet say: "As when a lion seizes and snatches its prey and roars over it, and the mountains are filled with its voice"? The Saviour himself speaks of nature: "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which is smaller than the other seeds; but when it has grown, it becomes greater than all the garden plants." And again: "The kingdom of heaven is as if a man should cast his seed, and it sprouts and grows, he himself does not know how; for the earth sprouts of its own accord, first the blade, then the ear, then it fills the grain in the ear." The Saviour also speaks about the sky: "If," he says, "the sky is red in the evening, you say, 'Fair weather, for the sky is red'; and in the morning, 'Storm today, for the sky is red and lowering.'" What need, then, was there for these things? I say this because of those who in their ignorance set out to make accusations. A discourse about God is underway, and you run away from a careful hearing of doctrine? Since, then, by the grace of God, our task is to speak about the creation of man, not as the subject deserves but as far as we are able, we must now come down to our subject.

The heaven had been adorned, the earth had been crowned with its fruits, the waters of the sea had been set apart, plants had sprung up, the irrational animals had come forth, the inhabited world had been filled, the house had been furnished. What was missing was the master of the house over all that had come into being. God said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." Yesterday we showed what the force of "let us make" is, whose word it is and to whom it is spoken, who the counselor is and whose the shared deliberation is. But since we showed from the Scriptures that the Son was the counselor of that ancient counsel, while we kept silent about the glory of the Holy Spirit, so that the sick might not get pretexts from us who are healthy, it is necessary to know that there is one glory, one mind, one effective word of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Here the Son is called counselor. Elsewhere it is said that no one has the knowledge of God except the Holy Spirit. Paul says: "No one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him; so also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." If the spirit in you is foreign to your own essence, then the Spirit in God is foreign to God's essence.

Does the Father will something? The Son and the Holy Spirit will the same. Does the Son will something? The Father and the Spirit will the same. Does the Spirit will something? The Father and the Son will the same. Does the Father raise the dead? The Son raises them too. The Saviour says: "For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." See how their will is joined together. Where, then, is the will of the Spirit? Listen: "All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as he wills." There is one kingdom of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. God also rebukes those who try to do anything without God's consent. He says through the prophet: "Woe to you, rebellious children, says the Lord. You have made a plan, but not through me, and covenants, but not through my Spirit." The prophet Zechariah clearly presented the Holy Trinity when he said: "Let the hands of Zerubbabel be strong, says the Lord, and let the hands of Jozadak the priest be strong, and the hands of the people, for I am with you, says the Lord, and my good word, and my Spirit is in your midst." Besides, brothers, our rebirth bears witness to the creation. If the Spirit had not shared with the Father and the Son in the creation, he would not have shared in the rebirth. How are we baptized? In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Which birth is greater, that of creation or that of initiation into the mysteries? There, life began and led to death; here, death begins and leads to life. How then can it be that in the greater work the Holy Spirit is a partner of the Father and the Son, but in the creation of the body he is cut off from their shared dignity? We would not have been created had we not been formed by the Holy Spirit. And since he is a partner of the Father and the Son in the first creation, he is likewise their partner and co-worker in baptism. Again, in the resurrection it is not possible for us to rise in any other way than by the Father willing, the Son working with him, and the Holy Spirit giving power. Listen to the Lord saying it. I was right to say "the Lord": even if it is Paul's voice, it is still the Lord's voice. For you can hear him say: "Since you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me." So the one who speaks in Paul says: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone does not have the Spirit of God, he does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Christ dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you." Without the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit there is no first creation, no second birth, no final resurrection. "Let us make man."

Here, then, I have protected myself in advance against the fault-finders. The word for "man" in the Hebrew language is interpreted as "fire." Pay attention, I beg you. The one who listens sincerely, as a friend and companion of the truth, is saved. But the one whose ears are hostile does not look for what will benefit him but for something to seize on, not for what he may gain but for what he may criticize. In the Hebrew tongue man is called fire. This name was not given to Adam for nothing. There are four elements in the world (again I am talking about nature, whether they like it or not): earth, water, air and fire. Each of the other elements stays as it is. For example, if you take a clod of earth, you cannot add to it out of what you hold; so if you take a clod of earth, it stays what it is. Again, if you take water by some measure, it stays the same water and receives no increase. If you fill a wineskin with air, another wineskin cannot be filled from it. But fire does not stay as it is. A small lamp is lit, and from it you kindle countless torches, a whole furnace, a great flame. It does not stay in its original appearance; fire grows with however much fuel it receives. So since God foreknew that the ends of the world would be filled from one human body (one lamp kindles so many torches, west and east and north and south), he gave a name worthy of the reality. For this reason the very name of Adam was a pledge of the whole world. Since the four regions were to be filled from him, he gives him the name Adam: A for Anatole, the east; D for Dysis, the west; A for Arktos, the north; M for Mesembria, the south. Both the name and its letters bear witness to man, who was to fill the world. So in the Hebrew language he is called fire. And since man bears the name of fire, Scripture does not hesitate to call the angels men as well. When the women with Mary came to the tomb, it says: "Behold, two men stood by them." But they were angels. And angels are also called fire: "He who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire." It calls them men because they share the same idea as man. And why are you surprised? God himself is called fire and is called man. The Saviour says about his own Father: "There was a man, a householder, who planted a vineyard. And he sent his servants, and the servants were killed." And, to cut it short: "And that man said: I still have one son; I will send him; perhaps they will respect him." What does "man" mean when applied to the divine name? For he did not speak by way of comparison. He did not say "is like," but "there was a man." That is why Moses says: "Our God is a consuming fire." And the Saviour, when he came, says: "I came to cast fire upon the earth." So man receives a name worthy of the reality. Since fire, as I said earlier, grows great from something small, and man from small beginnings filled the ends of the world, man was called fire. This is because of "let us make man": for in Hebrew it is "let us make fire."

"Let us make man in our image." Many simple people, whose souls are untrained, have supposed that man is in the image of God as though God had a nose, or eyes like ours, or ears like ours, or a mouth like ours. But this notion is mistaken and absurd. And to this day there is a heresy that says the divine has human form. Because they heard "the eyes of the Lord," "the ears of the Lord," "the Lord smelled," "the mouth of the Lord has spoken," "the hand of the Lord made," and "the feet of God stood," they pictured the incorporeal with limbs, not realizing how absurd the notion was. God speaks so that you may learn that man bears no resemblance to God as far as bodily appearance goes. I am not doing away with the word that says "let us make man in the image"; rather, it is being shown in what sense God says "in the image." "I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord." And again the same: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet." Shall we follow the letter? Shall we be slaves to the word? But the logic of it refutes me. How am I to understand heaven as a throne? A throne encloses the one sitting on it, but God is not circumscribed. Nothing surrounds God; God encircles and walls in all things. If, then, he has heaven as his throne, how will he measure heaven with a span of his hand? And how does he sit in heaven? "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet." Where does he sit? On the visible heaven? The stars are below the firmament, and water is above it. If he sits above, then it is not above the heavens but in the higher heaven. And if he sits at all, then his feet must hang down to the earth. Do you put such a shape on the one who has no shape? Is it not impious even to think this way? And then, if his feet tread on the earth, how do we sow? How do we reap? How do we walk about without bumping into his feet? And how did he measure heaven with a span? How did he have huge fingers in proportion to his divinity? And how, with fingers like those, did he write on small tablets, and with only a few of those fingers? We write with three fingers while the others help; God wrote the tablets with one finger. Have you ever seen anyone write with one finger? These things are meant to be understood with the mind rather than taken by the letter.

"Let us make man in our image." God wants us to imitate him in virtue. What does "in the image" mean? God is holy; if we become holy, we are in the image of God. For "Be holy, because I am holy." God is just; if we pursue justice, we are the image of God. For "the Lord is just and has loved justice." If we are kind and merciful, we are the image of God. For the Saviour says, "Be merciful, as your Father is merciful." Do you see where the image lies? Paul too points out the image. For he says, "Put off the old man and put on the new, which was created according to God for the knowledge of the truth, after the image of the one who created him." Do you see that "in our image" is ascribed to the virtues? In what else is the image? In authority, again: "Let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the wild beasts and the creeping things and the cattle and all the earth." Oh, the order God keeps! Oh, the precision of the words! Why did he first mention "Let them rule over the fish of the sea"? The order of dominion follows the order of creation. Since the fish and the birds came first, out of the sea, and after them the four-footed beasts and the other cattle from the earth, he therefore names first what came into being first: "Let them rule over the fish and the birds and the wild beasts and the creeping things and the cattle." That is why the three youths, too, as they bless God in the furnace, keep the same order: "Bless the Lord, you seas and rivers. Bless the Lord, you whales and all that move in the waters. Bless the Lord, all you birds of the sky. Bless him, you wild beasts and cattle. Bless him, you children of men." There are other things we could consider, but let us return to our subject. "And God formed man." He did not simply say "made" but "formed." "Forming" is said with regard to comeliness, as when someone who sees a handsome face says it is a fine piece of forming. God made nothing in the body unseemly; everything serves both comeliness and use. The eye, for instance, has both use and comeliness: it sees, it brightens the face, it adorns the countenance, and it beholds all things. The ear has its use, and it has its appearance, for the cymbal-like shell set around it adorns the creature. Likewise the nose has the sense of smell, which is necessary; but, unlike the other animals, it also has a kind of dividing wall that completes its comeliness. This belongs to man; for the other animals do not have nostrils so divided, but a single opening overall. God formed it so for this very reason. That is why David says, "He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?" So too he made the earth for comeliness and for use. And so as not to show you many comely features, I will mention one and pass on. Along with everything else, God gave man—I mean the male—well-proportioned breasts. Why breasts for a man? For comeliness. For a woman, granted, they exist out of natural necessity, to supply milk. But why breasts for a man? For comeliness, for good order. Just as in buildings some things are made out of necessity and some for comeliness, so God both adorned man and fitted him out for use. "He formed him, taking dust from the earth." Blessed are the hopes of Christians, if we understand what we hear! Why did it not say, "He took a clod from the earth"? He formed so great a body, and he did not need even a clod; he takes dust. God foresaw the future as though it were present. Since he foreknew that this creature would die and turn into dust, he anticipated it in the act of creation and showed the hope of the resurrection. He takes dust from the earth so that when you see dust in a tomb, you may know that the one who formed that dust also raises this. "He formed man, taking dust from the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life." See the difference between human beings and the irrational animals. When God made all the others, he brought forth the soul together with the body, all at once. Pay attention, I beg you. He made the swimming creatures, body and soul together: "Let the earth bring forth living creatures." The soul came forth together with the bodies. Man he makes first in his body, then in his soul. For what hope? As the forming is, so is the dissolution. Animals have no resurrection for this reason: as they came into being, so they die; body and soul vanish together. Man's body God took from the earth, but the soul he gives himself, creating and fashioning it, not casting it out of his own substance, so that when the body—or the man—dies, we may not despair of the soul. For what if the body has been buried in a tomb? Do not expect the soul to be there. It was not taken from the earth, and it does not go back into the earth. So he established our hope. That is why in Ezekiel, too, he prophesies the resurrection, saying: the dead bones received a body. Then he says, "Let the spirit come from the four winds and enter these dead, and let them live." So too David cries out: "You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth." Do you see the Spirit as creator? Do you see him as God's fellow worker?

But let us return to our subject. "He breathed into." By "he breathed into" he showed the simplicity of the soul; that is why it is not composed of many parts either. Now pay attention. Since creation had grown old, Christ renews it in his dispensation. Adam was formed from earth; Christ formed the blind man's eyes from clay, so that you might recognize the one who took dust from the earth and formed man. God breathed the breath of life into Adam's face; Christ breathed into the faces of the apostles and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." The breath that Adam lost, Christ here gave back, and man once again became a living soul. Pay attention here to the sequence. For even though the instrument of my voice is weary, I press on in my usual hope and, anticipating the prayers of the brethren, I trust that speech will be given me—not because of my own worth, but because of the eagerness of those who listen. Even if we are unworthy of the saints, they too suffered such things and were hindered by the weakness of the body. David bears witness, saying, "I grew weary with crying out; my throat became hoarse." Better to say what is right with a hoarse voice than to have a sound voice and a twisted soul. "God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east." What is Eden? Eden means "delight," as if one were to say, "He planted a paradise in delight," that is, in a delightful place, in a beautiful place. That is why at the end it says, "And he cast out Adam and settled him opposite the paradise of delight." "God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east." Why was paradise placed toward the east and not in some other region? Where the course of the heavenly lights begins, there too the course of human life began. God foretells what is to come. He places man in paradise toward the east to show that just as these lights rise and run toward the west and set, so man too must run from life to death and set, after the pattern of the lights, and then receive another rising through the resurrection of the dead. Adam ran toward the west; he set in the tomb. Earthly things followed him and were buried with the one who had set. Christ came and made the one who had set rise again. That is why the prophet says of him, "Behold a man whose name is Rising, and from beneath him he shall rise"—that is, from the tombs. In Adam man set; in Christ he rose. Paul bears witness: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." "And God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise." He brought him into a house made ready. Just as someone who invites a guest to a banquet first prepares the house and then brings in the one invited, so it is here. He prepared paradise for him as a fitting dwelling, and so brought in the one invited. Where was he formed? On the earth, outside paradise. For just as the lights were made elsewhere and then set in the sky, so Adam was formed outside, in another land, and then brought into paradise. How do we know this? Scripture says at the end, when Adam was being cast out: "And God sent Adam out of the paradise of delight to till the ground from which he was taken." "He placed him in the paradise of delight to work it and to keep paradise." To work it—for what was lacking in paradise? And even if a laborer had been needed, where would a plough have come from? Where the other implements of farming? To work and to keep God's commandment, and to believe God's commandment—that was his work. The Saviour says, "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." Just as believing in Christ is a work, so was believing the commandment: that if he touched it he would die, but if he did not touch it he would live. Keeping the spiritual words was his work. What was Paul's work? Was Paul a farmer? Did he have some other trade? Was not his whole work the word? Was it not preaching? And he says to his disciples, "You are my work in the Lord." It says he was to work it and to keep it. Keep it from whom? There was no robber, no passer-by, no plotter. From whom was he to keep it? So that he might keep it for himself, so that he might not lose it by transgressing, but by keeping the commandment keep paradise for himself. My mind grows weary along with my voice; but let us give ourselves to the meaning. He placed him in paradise. From here on, Scripture sketches what is to come through what came before. "A river goes out of Eden to water paradise." From this learn that paradise was not a little garden of small extent. So great a river waters it that its overflow makes four rivers. "A river goes out of Eden to water paradise." From there, after watering it, it divides into four heads: into the Tigris, into the Nile, into the Euphrates, and into the river called in Scripture the Pishon, which they now call the Danube.

See the size of a river that divides into four! And such a river waters paradise alone. Why so great a river? Adam was alone; what need was there for so much? But it was not made for one man only, but for the ends of the inhabited world. It was being prepared for patriarchs, prophets, apostles, evangelists, martyrs, confessors, saints, the faithful, the orthodox, those who live piously, for all the righteous. For if the Saviour promised paradise to the thief who confessed him in a single hour, saying, "Today you will be with me in paradise," what of one who has toiled from his youth? Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the patriarchs descended from him—and yet before all of these the thief inherits paradise. So God makes his works not with a view to what is seen, but to what is expected. Why did he make the earth so broad? For Adam, or for those who now inhabit it? "From there it is divided into four heads." It did not say "into four branches," but "heads," that is, springs. "The name of the one is Pishon," which we just mentioned; then the Gihon—this is the Nile; Gihon is its ancient name. Jeremiah bears witness, saying, "What have you to do with the road to Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon?" Pay attention here. Imagine this is paradise—for things are conveyed better by sight than by words. A great river comes forth with an abundant stream and waters paradise. From there it is carried into some underground chasm and sinks beneath a boundless stretch of earth, as the Master who laid out its path knows; and the stream stays hidden for a long way and wells up in various places, and one is found in Ethiopia, another in the west, another in the east, God thus drawing the stream through an underground channel and making strange springs for the first river. Why this? So that people might not follow the tracks of the rivers and find paradise, so that it might not be within human reach. For if it could be reached by travelling, no one would have found paradise before the rich. But God shut it off from poor and rich alike, so that they might find the way by virtue alone. How much did patriarchs, prophets and saints toil in seeking paradise, and they did not find it! The thief, without travelling the road but by believing, truly found the way—the one who says, "I am the way." He found paradise, which disobedience had shut against the first man. Now I ask the reason why the historian, in mentioning the first river, said that there is found "the fine gold, and the carbuncle, and the green stone." If he were describing the geography of the whole inhabited world, he ought to have named the fine things found in each region: the emeralds, the jacinths, where the topaz is found, where the various kinds of materials [?]. But he mentions gold and two stones, the firstfruits of the priesthood, since the priest wore a golden plate on which the name of God was inscribed. There were twelve stones on the priest's breast: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, onyx. Of these twelve stones the green stone was assigned to the priestly tribe and the carbuncle to the royal tribe. Why? Because it is the property of fire to burn and to give light, and the property of a king to do good and to punish. He places Reuben, the first tribe, on the sardius, Simeon on the topaz, Levi on the green stone, and Judah, from whom came Christ, on the fiery-red carbuncle. Indeed, Isaiah many years later says to Jerusalem: "I have painted your walls on my hands, and you are continually before me. Behold, I am preparing the carbuncle as your stone"—meaning the Saviour. For he says, "Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone, chosen, precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." The carbuncle, then, is assigned to the royal tribe, the green stone (prasinos) to the priestly; for to act well (prattein kalōs) belongs to the priesthood. From that river four sources of rivers are divided off. Why then is their water not the same? For the studious ask: if they come from one river, or from one spring, why do they not all have one quality? What is the answer? They take on something of the soil and of the quality of the places through which they pass. Just as water itself has one nature and quality, but if it is steeped with wormwood it takes on one quality, with dill another, with rue another—the nature is one, but the materials change it—so it is with the rivers: since they travel through different places, one through soil of one quality, another through soil of another, they take on the quality of those places.

Having given the rivers their qualities through the position of the places, he next makes in paradise "every tree beautiful to see and good for food." He removed in advance the transgressor's excuse. Since it says of the woman that "the woman saw the tree, that it was beautiful to see and good for food," so that no one should think that this tree alone was comely compared with the others, he attested this excellence to all of them—that they were pleasing to the eye and very beautiful—so that you may learn that it was not out of want that he transgressed, but that he turned aside though he had abundance. "And the tree of life," it says, "in the middle of paradise, and the tree of knowing good and evil." There are three kinds of trees: some were given him so that he might live, some so that he might live well, and some so that he might live forever. He had life from those he permitted; he had the good life from the one he forbade. For to live well was to touch those he did not forbid and not to touch the one he forbade. This was living well: obeying God. The tree of life stood in the middle like a prize, the tree of knowledge like a wrestling bout, like a training ground. If you kept the commandment concerning this tree, you would receive the prize. And see the marvel. All the trees of paradise round about were everywhere leafy, everywhere teeming; only the two in the middle were a training ground and a stadium. Those round about were for food. But the matter of the transgression and of the tree must be saved for another occasion. Our present subject is this: God brings all the animals to Adam. Let the heretics listen. And do not be surprised if through every phrase and every word the argument is aimed at the heretics. For those who exalt themselves against the glorified kingdom are accused on every occasion. "The stone cries out from the wall." I do not speak of a word: not one iota or one stroke of Scripture leaves the heretics blameless. By everything they are accused who deny the Master of all. So pay attention. It was a strange sight: Adam standing, and God, like a servant, bringing things to Adam. For God brought the animals. Here pay attention not to the wording but to the sense. Picture God standing and Adam examining. God brought them all forward and said to Adam: "Come, say, what do you think this one should be called?" "Let it be called lion." God, it says, confirmed it. Then: "And this one, what is it?" "Let it be called bull." "You have assigned it well." In the same way God set his seal on each of the names given. For Scripture says, "He brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. And whatever Adam called it, that was its name." See: since he had made him in his image, he wanted to bring his honor into view and to show truly that he bears the image of wisdom. And see the marvel. God had determined the names for himself beforehand, but he wanted it shown through the image that Adam's judgments agreed with God's will. Indeed, wishing to show that what Adam assigned God had predetermined, Scripture says, "And whatever Adam called them, that was its name"—that is, this had been predetermined; God had so decided.

But let us return to our subject. Adam stands, and God brought the animals before him. And the Master is not dishonored by bringing them to the servant. Yet if the heretics hear that Christ brings us to the Father, they immediately say, "You see that he is a servant?" "He brought them to Adam." The servant stood judging and the Master bringing. And God was not dishonored in bringing things to Adam; yet if they hear of Christ bringing us to the Father, they drag him down to a servant's rank. If the Saviour says, "No one comes to the Father except through me," at once the heretics prick up their ears—or rather twist them. God, in bringing the animals to Adam, is not his servant. If God brings a human being to God, does he hold a servant's rank? And lest ignorance of the texts feed your disease, I know both of the Son bringing people to the Father and of the Father bringing them to the Son. For he who said, "No one comes to the Father except through me," also said, "No one comes to me unless my heavenly Father draws him." I know I have said this before, but the saying is akin to our subject; and it may be that some did not hear it then, so I say it now. Consider how many four-footed beasts there are. Consider the tame, the wild, those in the mountains, those in the plains, those in Gaul, those in India, those in every region of the inhabited world; and again the creeping things, their kinds and species, all the birds, the swimming creatures, all those in the sea, in lakes, in rivers. All these were brought before him, and Adam gave each a name. And God did not object, but abided by them. Myriads of names, and God goes along with them. God speaks one name, bearing witness from heaven—"This is my Son"—and the heretics reject the voice that bore witness with one name, that holy voice which accepted countless names and did not alter them. The animals were brought and were named. And so he stood as a king.

Just as soldiers, when they enlist, are marked with the royal seal, so, since he was about to hand over dominion to him, he has him give names as master. For no one gives names but a master or a father. Pay attention. Of the names, some God gave, some Adam. God called heaven, earth, sea, firmament, day, light, night, fruit, herb, grass, trees; but the cattle and the birds Adam named: peacock, eagle, calf, sheep. Adam named the species, God the genera, so that the word of the one who said, "Let us make man in our image," might not prove false. God gives names to the heavenly lights: the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades, Hesperus the light-bearer. All these God named. David bears witness, saying, "He who numbers the multitudes of the stars and calls them all by name." God names the things above, Adam the things on earth. God names heaven, earth, all the rest; he calls Adam "fire" [?], "man." What does Adam name? He gives names to the cattle, the birds, the creeping things, the wild beasts.

Adam uses an unfamiliar name, bone and flesh, when he says of the woman: "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." For when God formed him, God did not say that he had formed him out of bones and flesh. Again, God says "male," but Adam says "man"; God says "female," but Adam says "woman." And here is the wonderful thing: since he had been filled with the Holy Spirit, and the poor man had not yet transgressed but was full of grace, the whole of prophecy, which I divided into its parts a few days ago before you, my beloved, was present in him. For he knew what had gone before, and he knew what was present and what was to come. How did he know what was present? A bone cannot be seen from outside the body. But because he had the Spirit, he says: "This now is bone of my bones." How did he know, unless the Holy Spirit revealed it? Why, then, does he say bone first and then flesh? Because it was a rib that God first took from him. "She," he says, "shall be called woman, because she was taken out of her man." He prophesies what had gone before; he has spoken of what was present; now he speaks of what is to come: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother." There was as yet no marriage, so where would a father and mother come from? Again, let the heretics listen. God wished to make the woman for Adam. He cast a trance upon Adam, and he slept. Every word of God became an ancient rule of nature. From the very first he taught how a new creature must be divided off from a human being. God cast sleep upon Adam. A wonderful thing! Scripture is speaking of the time at which marriage takes place. Sleep is called a trance, because a person stands, as it were, outside himself. The soul is within, and yet it is not within. It does not perceive, it does not understand; it hears and yet does not hear. Just as we say today, "He fell into a trance," meaning he was outside of things, so the soul, when it is outside the senses, is in a trance. "And he slept," it says, "and God took one of his ribs." Let the heretics be asked about these things. How did God take it? How did Adam feel no pain? How was he not hurt? If a single hair is pulled from the body, we are hurt. Even if someone is sound asleep, the sleeper is woken by the pain. So large a member is lifted out, so large a rib is torn away, and the sleeper does not wake? God did not wrench it out by force so that he would wake; he did not tear it away. But Scripture, wishing to show how quickly the Craftsman worked, says: "He took" [?]. The joints were loosened, and he did not feel it?

He took the rib just as he had taken the dust. If the one who joined the body together had been different from the one who loosened it, there would have been a struggle. But since the one who bound it was the one who loosened it, he loosened it somehow gently. He took the rib and filled up its place with flesh. From where did he fill it up? Did he draw it from the rest of the body? But every body that is drawn upon becomes thinner. How did he fill it up? We speak about the body and do not understand it; do we then speak about God and pry into his ways? "And the Lord built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman." How were eyes fashioned from a rib? How a heart that reasons? How a tongue that speaks? How were intestines stretched out from a rib? How did a liver come from a rib? You cannot grasp how these things came about, and yet you pry into the Craftsman? Rather, see the image of Christ everywhere. God did not take the rib from Adam until he had cast sleep upon him. Why? From a rib sin was to arise, the sin that entered through the woman. The Savior came, bringing water and blood from his side: water washing away sins, blood granting us the mystery. See the type. When Adam slept, the rib was taken. When sleep came upon the body of Christ, his side was opened, so that he might undo the ancient tragedy by the new story. By sleep I mean the sleep on the cross. He built the rib into a woman; he brought her to Adam. Oh, the love of the Master for humankind! How much he does: he forms, he bestows his kindness! He brings the animals before Adam; he leads the bride to him. For since Adam was like an orphan, and Eve likewise was a virgin, having no father or mother to fill that role, God fills the role of father and mother. And see the law. For every utterance of God is an ancient rule of nature. God brought the woman to Adam, and this has remained a law to this day: that the woman is given to the man. He does not escort the man as a bridegroom to the woman. "They were naked and were not ashamed." The rule remains; the law cries aloud. A man feels shame before everyone except his own wife. A woman feels modesty before everyone except her own husband. That much I have said with reference to the law; but the reason they were not ashamed of their nakedness is this: they were clothed with immortality and arrayed in glory. The glory did not allow their nakedness to be seen, for it covered their nakedness. Where can you again see a man who is naked and not ashamed? You find him in Christ. Peter and John and James came to the tomb looking for the body, and did not find it; but they found the clothes rolled up, so that it might be shown that after the resurrection of Christ the original state of Adam is preserved in him: he is without clothes, yet not naked but clothed. Christ rose and took off the clothes that Adam had put on, and he was naked, yet he was not seen to be naked. After the resurrection the women see the clothes cast aside. Martha and Mary see him, recognize him, fall at his feet, and do not see him naked. Where did he get clothes to wear? For he had cast them off in the tomb, and the soldiers had divided his earlier garments. How, then, is he clothed? How is the naked one not naked? And I ask something else as well. Why did they see the clothes and the linen sheet in one place, and the face-cloth with which the Savior's head had been bound in a place by itself? So that holy grace might show that the resurrection did not happen in commotion. And since the Jews were going to spread the rumor that he had been stolen by the disciples, he leaves his clothes in the tomb. For whoever steals a corpse steals it along with its clothes. One could see the Savior going out of the tomb as Joseph went out of the house of the Egyptian woman. And see the difference. After the resurrection Christ was seen naked, and Peter was naked too. But the one had immortality, while the other was still mortal. Jesus stood on the shore, clothed in glory, and said: "Children, have you anything to eat?" "No," they say, "we have nothing." For they did not recognize him. Then he says: "Cast the net on the right side of the boat." They cast it and caught a great multitude of fish. John recognizes him and says to Peter: "It is the Lord." Oh, the wonder! They did not recognize him by his voice, but by his works. "And Peter," it says, "put on his outer garment, for he was naked." The mortal body is ashamed; the immortal is not ashamed. But let us fall down before him who clothed us with glory, who clothed the world with immortality; let us implore him to clothe us with faith, with the hope of salvation, with the glory that is in Christ. For to the Father be glory, with the only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
